parole.significato: to authorize (grant approval or permission for, especially the distribution or reproduction of texts)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin auctōrizāre. Compare Russian авторизова́ть (avtorizovátʹ), Polish autoryzować.

parole.significato: agglomeration (the act or process of collecting in a mass; a heaping together)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin agglomerātiō. Compare Russian агломера́ция (aglomerácija), Belarusian агламера́цыя (ahlamjerácyja), Polish aglomeracja.

parole.significato: adaptation (process of adapting something or becoming adapted to a situation)
parole.testo: Derived via Western European languages from Medieval Latin adaptātiō, from Latin adaptō. Compare Russian адапта́ция (adaptácija), Belarusian адапта́цыя (adaptácyja), Polish adaptacja. By surface analysis, адапт- (adapt-) + -ація (-acija)
From Medieval Latin algorismus, from Arabic الخَوَارِزْمِيّ (al-ḵawārizmiyy), the nisba of Persian mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā priōrī (“involving reasoning from cause to effect; from first principles”, literally “from the former”). Compare Russian априо́ри (aprióri), Belarusian апрыёры (apryjóry).

parole.significato: a male theological school in XVIII-XIX centuries
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bursa or Polish bursa. For senses related to schooling, compare to English burse (“fund for students”). Doublet of бі́ржа (bírža).
Ultimately from Medieval Latin virtuālis, from virtus (“virtue”), with -альний (-alʹnyj) ending. Compare Russian виртуа́льный (virtuálʹnyj), Belarusian віртуа́льны (virtuálʹny), Polish wirtualny.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin diamas from Latin adamas.
From Medieval Latin exhumātiō, from exhumō (“to exhume”), from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”). Compare Russian эксгума́ция (eksgumácija), Belarusian эксгума́цыя (ekshumácyja), Polish ekshumacja.
From Medieval Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ).
From Medieval Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδημία (epidēmía).

parole.significato: zenith (point in the sky vertically above a given position or observer; the point in the celestial sphere opposite the…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cenit, from Arabic سَمْت (samt, “direction, path”). Compare Russian зени́т (zenít), Polish zenit.

parole.significato: receipt (written acknowledgment that a specified article or sum of money has been received)
parole.testo: Derived from Medieval Latin quitantia, from Latin quiētantia. Compare Russian квита́нция (kvitáncija), Belarusian квіта́нцыя (kvitáncyja), Polish kwitacyja.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin connotātiō, from connotō (“to mark in addition”). Compare Russian коннота́ция (konnotácija), Belarusian каната́цыя (kanatácyja), Polish konotacja.

From Medieval Latin cosmologia, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + -λογία (-logía). With -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending. Compare Russian космоло́гия (kosmológija), Belarusian касмало́гія (kasmalóhija), Polish kosmologia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin laboratorium.
Derived via Western European languages from Medieval Latin legenda, from Latin legō.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin metaphysica, from Byzantine Greek μεταφυσική (metaphusikḗ), from the Ancient Greek title of the collection by Aristotle τὰ μετὰ τὰ φυσικά (tà metà tà phusiká). Compare Russian метафи́зика (metafízika), Belarusian метафі́зіка (mjetafízika).
Derived via Western European languages from Medieval Latin necrologium.

parole.significato: lens, objective (object, usually made of glass, that focuses or defocuses the light that passes through it)
parole.testo: Derived via Western European languages (compare French objectif and German Objektiv), ultimately from Medieval Latin objectīvus. Compare Belarusian аб’екты́ў (abʺjektýw), Russian объекти́в (obʺjektív) and Polish obiektyw.

parole.significato: objective (based on observed facts without subjective assessment)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin objectīvus. Compare Russian объекти́вный (obʺjektívnyj), Belarusian аб'екты́ўны (abʺjektýwny), Polish obiektywny. Morphologically analyzable as об'єкти́в (obʺjektýv, “objective”) + -ний (-nyj, adjective-forming suffix).
Ultimately from Medieval Latin opticus (“optic, optical”), from Ancient Greek ὀπτικός (optikós).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin paranoia, from Ancient Greek παράνοια (paránoia).
From Old East Slavic поганъ (poganŭ, “pagan”), borrowed from Medieval Latin paganus (“pagan”).
From Medieval Latin punctuālis. Compare Russian пунктуа́льный (punktuálʹnyj), Belarusian пунктуа́льны (punktuálʹny), Polish punktualny.
From Medieval Latin ratificātiō. Compare Russian ратифика́ция (ratifikácija), Belarusian ратыфіка́цыя (ratyfikácyja), Polish ratyfikacja.

From Medieval Latin rehabilitātio. Compare Russian реабилита́ция (reabilitácija), Belarusian рэабіліта́цыя (reabilitácyja), Polish rehabilitacja. By surface analysis, ре- (re-) + абіліт- (abilit-) + -ація (-acija)
Borrowed from Medieval Latin repatriātio, from Latin repatriō, with -а́ція (-ácija) suffix. Compare Russian репатриа́ция (repatriácija), Belarusian рэпатрыя́цыя (repatryjácyja), Polish repatriacja.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rēptilia. Compare Russian репти́лия (reptílija), Belarusian рэпты́лія (reptýlija).
From Medieval Latin certificātiō. Compare Russian сертифика́ция (sertifikácija), Belarusian сертыфіка́цыя (sjertyfikácyja), Polish certyfikacja.
From Medieval Latin signāle, noun use of the neuter of Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum.
Ultimately from Medieval Latin signāle. Compare Belarusian сігналізава́ць (sihnalizavácʹ), Polish sygnalizować, Russian сигнализи́ровать (signalizírovatʹ).
Ultimately derived from Medieval Latin specificatio. Compare Russian специфика́ция (specifikácija), Polish specyfikacja.

Derived via Western European languages from Medieval Latin sporadicus, from Ancient Greek σποραδικός (sporadikós). Compare Russian споради́ческий (sporadíčeskij), Belarusian спарады́чны (sparadýčny), Polish sporadyczny.
Derived via Western European languages from Medieval Latin sublīmātiō. Compare Russian сублима́ция (sublimácija), Belarusian субліма́цыя (sublimácyja), Polish sublimacja.

parole.significato: seniority, subordination (the quality of being properly obedient to a superior; this quality as a systemic principle of…
parole.testo: Derived via Western European languages from Medieval Latin subōrdinātiō, from Latin subōrdinō. Compare Russian субордина́ция (subordinácija), Belarusian субардына́цыя (subardynácyja), Polish subordynacja.
Ultimately from Medieval Latin terminus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trivium.

parole.significato: to characterize (depict someone or something a particular way)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin charactērizō, from Ancient Greek χαρακτηρίζω (kharaktērízō, “to designate by a characteristic mark”), from χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “a mark, character”). With -ува́ти (-uváty) ending. Compare Russian характеризова́ть (xarakterizovátʹ), Belarusian характарызава́ць (xaraktaryzavácʹ), P

parole.significato: lawyer (professional person qualified to practise law)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin iūrista, possibly via Russian юри́ст (juríst).

parole.significato: set of instruments, toolset, toolkit, instrumentarium
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin īnstrūmentārium. Compare Russian инструмента́рий (instrumentárij), Belarusian інструмента́рый (instrumjentáryj), Polish instrumentarium.

parole.significato: stroke (a sudden interruption of blood supply to the brain, causing minor to major brain damage and possible death; it…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin īnsultus.

Borrowed from Western European languages, ultimately from Medieval Latin intuitivus, from Latin intueri. Compare Russian интуити́вный (intuitívnyj), Belarusian інтуіты́ўны (intuitýwny), Polish intuicyjny.

Borrowed from Western European languages, ultimately from Medieval Latin intuitio (“a looking at, immediate cognition”), from Latin intueri (“to look at, consider”), from in (“in, on”) + tueri (“to look, watch, guard, see, observe”).
